newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila stocks seen drifting despite economic joy.
newsitem.headline: Manila stocks seen drifting despite economic joy.

text.p: The Manila stock market jumped on Thursday after the government announced lower-than-expected inflation figures for November, but analysts said that was a knee-jerk reaction and was unlikely to be sustained.
Shares ended several days of drifting, with the main index shooting up 32.46 points, or 1.04 percent, to 3,163.33.
Brokers attributed the rise to news that November inflation had fallen to 4.5 percent, lower than the market expectations of around 5.7 percent. In October, the rate was 4.7 percent.
The inflation news comes a week after the government said the gross national product grew 7.1 percent in the first nine months of the year, up from a 5.3 percent in the same period last year.

But analysts said the two factors were not enough to take the market out of its year-end lethargy, even though the main stock index has risen 73.17 points, or 2.36 percent, since the beginning of the month.
"After the two economic data, we don't expect any (further) corporate and economic news to perk up the market," said Angel Escalona, an analyst at Citibank Securities.
She said most investors would probably wait for early next year when full-year corporate results are due to be released.
The analysts said fund managers had cashed in their gains so they could report better financial statements.
"Some of them have already completed the process this early," Ramon Vicente Kabigting, general manager of PCIB Securities, told Reuters.

"It will be like flogging a dead horse," said Luz Lorenzo, economist at Peregrine Securities, when asked how the favourable economic statistics would affect the market's mood. "We've had good inflation figures in the past months. We've had good export figures, but the market hasn't responded."

She attributed the market's sluggishness to the fact that interest rates had not fallen as quickly as inflation. Domestic interest rates have been hovering between 11.3 and 13 percent all year despite a continued slide in the inflation rate.
However, Lorenzo said the recent decision to cut banks' reserve requirements by one percentage point could prompt early positioning into 1997. The reduction takes effect on January 3.
Kabigting said any uptick in share prices over the rest of the month would be solely due to punting.
"Any such movement is likely to be devoid of serious foreign participation... What we'll have are short-term players trying to position on blue chips in anticipation of foreign entry," he added.
